lines.text: Lesson seventeen: support, resistance, breakout and fakeout.
The price areas traders watch, and how to read them calmly.
In lesson sixteen, you marked swing highs and swing lows on a chart.
Look closely. Price keeps turning back near the same two areas.
Why does that happen? And what if price finally pushes through?
Support is a price area where falling price has stopped and turned up before.
Think of a floor. Price drops, lands on it, and bounces.
Here, price fell to about 59,850 three times. Each touch is called a test.
Buyers stepped in there before. That is all support tells you: what happened before.
Resistance is the opposite: an area where rising price has stopped and turned down.
Like a ceiling. Price climbs, bumps into it, and falls back.
Here, rallies stalled near 60,350 twice. Sellers were waiting there before.
An important detail: support and resistance are zones, not exact lines.
The three lows were 59,830, 59,860 and 59,880. Not one exact price.
So we draw a band from 59,800 to 59,900. That zone is 100 USDT tall.
Price can poke into a zone, or a little through it, without anything changing.
A breakout is when price closes beyond a zone and keeps going.
Our resistance zone runs from 60,300 to 60,400. Watch this candle.
It closes at 60,480: a full 80 USDT above the top of the zone.
Then price comes back to the zone from above. That's a retest. Here, it holds.
The old ceiling acted like a floor. This time.
Now the same chart, with a different ending.
A fakeout, or false breakout, is when price pokes beyond a zone, then falls back inside.
The wick reaches 60,460, but the candle closes at 60,350, back inside the zone.
Then price drops toward 60,150. Same past chart, two different futures.
So what counts as confirmation? Evidence that a breakout is holding.
One: a candle closes beyond the zone. A wick alone is not enough.
Two: the next candles stay beyond it, too.
Three: if price comes back for a retest, the zone holds.
Confirmation makes a breakout more believable. It never makes it certain.
A common mistake: drawing one exact line and expecting price to obey it.
Or jumping in the moment a wick crosses that line.
The fix: draw zones, wait for candles to close, and treat every level as a maybe.
And WAIT is always allowed. You never have to act on a level.
Your turn. The resistance zone is 60,300 to 60,400.
The last candle wicked to 60,450 but closed at 60,380. Is the breakout confirmed?
Not yet. The close, 60,380, is still 20 USDT inside the zone.
A sensible choice here is WAIT, and watch where the next candle closes.
One more warning. Liquidity means how many orders are waiting near the price.
When liquidity is thin, only a few small orders are waiting.
Then one larger order can jump price through a zone, and it snaps back moments later.
It looked like a breakout. It was just a thin market.
Before you use any of this, know the limits.
Lines come from past prices. They promise nothing about the future.
Fakeouts are common, thin markets can fake a breakout, and stops can slip.
Losses are always possible. WAIT is a decision, not a failure.
Let's recap.
Support and resistance are zones where price turned before. Not walls.
A breakout closes beyond a zone and holds. A fakeout falls back inside.
Confirmation is evidence, not certainty. WAIT is always allowed.
Check yourself: a wick crosses resistance, but the candle closes inside. Breakout?
Not confirmed. It could be a fakeout. Wait for a close beyond the zone.
Well done! Next up: volume, volatility and range. See you in lesson eighteen.
